title: Memory and context
description: The context window, why a model loses the thread of a long chat, and how an agent remembers you with three kinds of memory and a profile.

steps.text: Ever notice this? In a long chat the model suddenly loses the thread. In a new chat it doesn't remember what you talked about before, yet it still knows your name. It comes down to how its memory works.

steps.imagePrompt: A small robot with an empty thought bubble sits at a desk, while a helpful assistant beside it hands over a neat folder of notes taken from a filing cabinet.
steps.caption: The model forgets. The app remembers and hands over what's needed

steps.text: The model itself remembers nothing between requests. Each time it gets a package of text, answers, and right away “forgets” it. The memory belongs to the app, not the model. The app decides what to put in front of it next time.

steps.term: The app remembers, not the model
steps.definition: Between requests the model is empty. The app holds all the memory and decides what to put into the context this time.
steps.example: In a new chat the model knows your profile, because the app puts it into every chat. But it doesn't remember the old conversation, because that isn't put into the package.

steps.text: Short-term memory is the history of the current conversation. Each time, the app puts the earlier messages into the context window, the very package the model sees. As long as the conversation fits in the window, it feels like the model remembers everything.

But the window has a ceiling: how many tokens the model takes at once. Everything counts, both what goes in and its answer, including hidden reasoning. Muse Spark has a huge window, about a million tokens.

Still, running a million tokens through the model for every message is slow and expensive. So the app trims the history long before the limit, at about 48 thousand tokens. It keeps the first 8 messages, which usually hold the topic and the goal, and the last 40. The middle is dropped. A note marks the gap, but there is no summary. That's how the model “loses the thread” in a very long chat.

steps.caption: A simple window: the old messages slide off the edge (the app still holds the start of the chat). Scroll the conversation and turn on long-term memory

steps.text: So anything important has to be kept outside the window. Long-term memory is facts about you, stored as “key → value” pairs: for example, that you prefer tea to coffee. Before answering, the app looks for facts that match your message and puts them into the window.

steps.question: And how does a fact get into long-term memory in the first place?
steps.answer: The model saves it itself, with the Memory tool, when it decides the fact is worth remembering. Most often that's because you said “remember” or “I prefer…” outright. The conversation itself doesn't turn into facts. If the model doesn't call the tool, there is no fact.

steps.text: Episodic memory is what the agent did. Every tool call is saved as an episode with its outcome: “set an alarm for 7:30 — ok.” Episodes are recalled by time: what happened today, yesterday, last week. That way the agent can return to things that are no longer in the current conversation.

And there is a separate profile: what you told the app about yourself when you first met. The app puts it into every chat, so the model knows your name and your “about me” even in a new one. So an agent doesn't have one memory but a bundle of three, plus the profile.

steps.caption: Three kinds of memory: short-term lives in the window, long-term and episodes are added from outside

steps.instruction: Pick the kind of memory for each example:

pairs.term: The last 5 messages in the chat
Yesterday the agent set an alarm
The name you gave when you met

steps.text: Practice. After the lesson, tell me in an ordinary chat: “remember: I like short answers.” Tap the wrench icon in the chat header. In “Tool calls” you'll see a line “Memory: remember a fact.” Then open a new chat and ask: “what kind of answers do I like?” Short-term memory stayed in the old chat, but the fact made it across through long-term memory.

One more detail about your own agents: each one has its own compartment of memory. When you build an agent, its long-term and episodic memory live in a separate cell. It can't see other agents' memories and won't mix up your affairs between them. There is no shared pot: memory belongs to one specific agent.

The main point: the model doesn't remember on its own. The app remembers for it and decides what goes into the limited window: the profile, matching facts, recent actions and as much of the conversation as fits. What isn't put in doesn't exist for the model this time.

questions.q: Why doesn't the model remember the earlier conversation in a new chat?
options: The model stores nothing, and the app doesn't put another chat's history in front of it
A timer wipes the model's internal memory, so after a day it forgets everyone
A new chat goes through a different server that can't reach the old one
questions.explain: The model keeps no state between requests. For a new chat the app adds your profile and matching facts, but not the old conversation.

questions.q: Why do we need long-term memory if we already have short-term memory?
options: The context window is limited, so important things must be kept outside it or they fall out
Long-term memory is faster than short-term, so answers arrive sooner
Short-term memory costs more, so it's better not to use it
questions.explain: The window is finite and the middle of a long chat drops out. That's why important facts are kept outside the window.

questions.q: How is episodic memory different from facts?
options: Episodes are what the agent did, recalled by time; facts are lasting “key → value” pairs about you
They are the same thing; “episodes” is just a marketing name for the same table of facts
Episodes are stored in the provider's cloud, while facts stay locally on the device
questions.explain: Facts are pairs about you. Episodes are records of tool calls with their outcome, available by time.

questions.q: What does the app do with a very long chat?
options: Keeps the start and the end, drops the middle
Replaces the middle with a short summary
Deletes the oldest messages from the chat
questions.explain: The model gets the first 8 and the last 40 messages. The middle drops out, and a note marks the gap. The chat on your screen stays untouched.
